title: Compressing Nemotron-3.5-SuperVL-120B to 1.4bit With Cactus Quants
summary: Compressing Nemotron-3.5-SuperVL-120B with Cactus Quants to 1.418 effective bits per weight, including vision and MTP. The complete checkpoint occupies 22.06 GB.
body_markdown:
We compressed **Nemotron-3.5-SuperVL-120B with Cactus Quants** to **1.418 effective bits per weight** . The complete 124.45B-parameter checkpoint occupies **22.06 GB** , including its language backbone, vision tower, projector and multi-token prediction head.


[Cactus Quants](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=Q6FcVpI1SO) is the quantization method behind[Whistle](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/whistle) ,[Needle](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/needle) and[Mirage](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/mirage) . This release brings CQ to NVIDIA's large hybrid model, combining compact vector codes with a mixed precision allocation and kernels that consume the packed projections.


Across 18 reported benchmarks, the unweighted mean relative score reduction is **3.6%** . Long agentic coding is a substantial exception. DeepSWE falls from 24 solved tasks to seven and is reported separately below.

**36GB M5 Max MacBook Pro.** 512 prompt tokens, 128 output tokens. Median warmed batch-one decode across three runs, with verified MTP. Speed rounded from 46.7 tokens/s.


The[checkpoint and inference source](https://huggingface.co/Cactus-Compute/nemotron-3.5-120b-cq1.4bit) are available together. Cactus MLX runs the model on Apple silicon through the existing` cactus-compute` package. On a 36GB M5 Max MacBook Pro, the compressed model reaches approximately 47 tokens/s under the measured workload above.


## Cactus Quants on Nemotron


CQ stores compact codes for weight vectors together with the information needed to reconstruct their scale. In this checkpoint, projection rows are divided into groups of 128 weights. Reconstruction uses fixed lattice codebooks and a 128-point Hadamard transform, with group norms and row and column scales preserving magnitude.


The codes describe vectors jointly. A 1.5-bit allocation therefore does not require a fractional bit attached to an individual number. The corresponding packed representation uses 24 bits for each 16-value vector, or 24 bytes of codes for a 128-weight group. A BF16 group alone occupies 256 bytes. The norms and scales add storage, which is why we also report the complete-file rate.

This algebra is what connects the packed representation to an efficient projection kernel; it does not remove the approximation introduced by quantization.


Nemotron does not use one precision everywhere. Routed experts account for most of its parameters, so their up and down projections use 1.5-bit and 1-bit codes. Mamba input projections and the vocabulary output head use 2-bit codes. Attention, routers, Mamba output projections, embeddings and vision linears retain 4-bit codes. Small remaining tensors keep BF16 or FP32 storage. The allocation below combines all components, including MTP.


## What 1.418 bits includes


A code precision and a complete model's storage rate measure different things. This checkpoint uses mixed precisions. Its final effective rate includes codes, group norms, scales, codebooks, unquantized tensors and the safetensors header, across the backbone, vision components and MTP head.

## Running the compressed projections


The checkpoint stores CQ projections in their packed representation. Our custom Metal operations use those codes with their codebooks and scales. Native MLX attention handles attention computation, while the CQ loader handles this model's packed tensors. This is a custom checkpoint format rather than a stock MLX-LM quantization preset.


Fig. 2


### From packed weights to a token


The checkpoint retains compact CQ codes alongside the tensors needed to interpret them.


Figure 2.


A schematic of the CQ projection path. Signal timing and matrix sizes are illustrative; they are not a latency trace or a literal kernel schedule.


Verified MTP is enabled by default for greedy generation. The MTP head proposes tokens, and the target model checks them. The reported decode measurement includes this verification work. Acceptance rate and draft overhead determine whether speculation saves time; the presence of an MTP head alone is not a throughput guarantee. Add` --no-mtp` to compare the ordinary decode path on your own workload.


The measured memory footprint is specific to the text workload above. Longer contexts and image inputs can change memory use and latency. The Mac result does not establish that this checkpoint fits on an iPhone.


## Get started with Cactus MLX


Use an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 26 or newer and Python 3.12. Install the MLX extra from the existing Cactus package.


```text
pip   install   -U   'cactus-compute[mlx]'
```


### Generate text


Pass the Hugging Face repository name directly. The first run downloads the model; subsequent runs reuse the local cache.


```text
cactus-mlx   generate   \
--model   Cactus-Compute/nemotron-3.5-120b-cq1.4bit   \
--prompt   'Write a Python function is_prime(n).'   \
--max-tokens   256
```


### Ask about an image


```text
cactus-mlx   generate   \
--model   Cactus-Compute/nemotron-3.5-120b-cq1.4bit   \
--image   photo.jpg   \
--prompt   'Describe this image.'
```


Repeat` --image` for multiple images. Vision uses the tower and projector included in the same checkpoint.


### Serve a local API


```text
cactus-mlx   server   \
--model   Cactus-Compute/nemotron-3.5-120b-cq1.4bit   \
--port   8080
```


The server exposes an OpenAI-compatible chat API. It also accepts image content through` image_url` parts, including HTTP(S) and base64 data URLs.


```text
curl   http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions   \
-H   'Content-Type: application/json'   \
-d   '{
"model": "Cactus-Compute/nemotron-3.5-120b-cq1.4bit",
"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain a binary search."}],
"max_tokens": 128,
"temperature": 0
}'
```

SWE-bench Verified uses mini-swe-agent with no network. BF16 solves 307/500 tasks, 61.4%, and CQ solves 318/500, 63.6%. These are observed scores, not evidence that compression generally improves agent reliability.


The[model card](https://huggingface.co/Cactus-Compute/nemotron-3.5-120b-cq1.4bit) gives exact scores, task counts and the complete evaluation qualifications. Several matter when comparing these numbers with other reports. GSM8K uses flexible extraction. MMLU-ProX uses the Lite set in ten languages and strict language-specific answer patterns. GraphWalks retains prompts that fit a 262K context with a 100K output cap. SciCode has two prefilled setup steps missing class declarations, affecting both models. BigCodeBench's leaderboard-labelled rows use a chat path rather than the official completions setup. V* and MathVision use their documented image prompts and scorers at temperature 0.6 and top_p 0.95.


### Long agentic coding remains a weakness


DeepSWE with OpenCode and no network falls from 24 solved tasks for BF16 to seven for CQ. The model card reports 113 tasks, or 21.2% versus 6.2%; a saved CQ aggregate records 110 rather than 113. The three-task denominator discrepancy remains unresolved, and neither the benchmark average nor the chart includes DeepSWE.


This is a substantial observed loss on long engineering runs. A single agent run per configuration also leaves run-to-run variance unmeasured. We investigated possible mechanisms with smaller, controlled experiments, including matched repair prompts and activation interventions. The companion article,[Why quantization can break multi-step workflows](https://www.cactuscompute.com/blog/quantization-and-multi-step-workflows) , separates the effects those experiments demonstrate from what remains unknown about this release.


## Weights, code and citation


The[Hugging Face repository](https://huggingface.co/Cactus-Compute/nemotron-3.5-120b-cq1.4bit) contains the model, detailed evaluations and inference source.[Cactus MLX is distributed on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/cactus-compute/) as the` mlx` extra of` cactus-compute` . The command remains` cactus-mlx` so the same interface can accept a repository name or local model path.


Cactus code and contributions are Apache 2.0. Upstream model materials retain OpenMDW 1.1; the release includes both license texts. For the quantization method, see the[Cactus Quants paper](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=Q6FcVpI1SO) . The model card provides the release citation.
